newsitem.title: USA: North Dakota declared major disaster area.
newsitem.headline: North Dakota declared major disaster area.

text.p: President Bill Clinton on Sunday declared all of North Dakota a major disaster area, making victims of severe winter storms and blizzards eligible for federal emergency aid.
North Dakota Gov. Edward Schafer requested federal disaster assistance and Clinton agreed after reviewing an analysis of damage by the Federal Emergency Management Agency, FEMA said in a statement.

Under the terms of the disaster declaration, the federal government will pay part of the cost of clearing snow emergency routes to provide emergency access for vehicles and other emergency assistance, FEMA said.
Clinton's action made federal disaster relief funds available to local governments and individuals in all 53 counties in the state, including some Native American lands.
In North Dakota and elsewhere in the northern plains, hundreds of miles of highways remained snowbound, some blocked by drifts as high as 16 feet (4.8 metres).
Undetermined numbers of travelers were still stranded in shelters and truck stops in the region.
At least 31 people have died as a result of the Arctic freeze that invaded the central United States on Thursday, according to official reports.
To the south, fierce winter storms swept across northern New Mexico, closing parts of two major interstate highways and stranding hundreds of motorists.
The Arctic blast also hit the Texas and Oklahoma Panhandles and spread southeast, with snow falling in Dallas.
Police reported dozens of traffic accidents in New Mexico and west Texas although none of them were serious.

"It's snow on ice. It's treacherous out there," New Mexico state police officer Justin Segotta said. He said drifts of up to 10 feet (3 metres) had forced sections of I-25 and I-40 to close down for several hours at a time.
Two men died on Saturday when they fell through ice on a pond near Albuquerque and drowned.
But while the snow and icy conditions caused havoc on highways, skiers were delighted.

"We are ecstatic. We've received 42 inches (106 cm) of snow since yesterday and it is still coming down strong," said J.P. Rael, marketing manager for the Taos Ski Valley resort in northern New Mexico.
In northern California, more rain was forecast, but it was not expected to worsen flooding that has caused an estimated $1.6 billion in damages and eight deaths over the past two weeks.
